question: A FastAPI retrieval service opens a fresh connection to Azure Database for PostgreSQL for every request, runs one 4 ms vector query, and closes it. End-to-end p50 is 71 ms, and traces show roughly 60 ms per request spent on TCP setup, TLS negotiation and Entra token authentication. What is the correct change?
options: Create an async connection pool at application startup with a warm minimum size and acquire a connection from it per request
Cache each request's query results in memory for 60 seconds so most requests avoid opening a connection at all
Disable TLS on connections to the database because the traffic stays inside the virtual network
Move the vector query into a stored procedure so the round trip completes in a single server call
optionExplanations: Correct. Connection establishment — TCP handshake, TLS negotiation and authentication — is a fixed cost paid per connection, not per query, so the answer is to amortise it by keeping connections open in a pool. A warm minimum size means the first requests after a scale-out do not each pay the setup cost either.

Caching may help a read-heavy workload, but it changes freshness semantics and does nothing for cache misses, which still pay the full 60 ms. It is an optimisation layered on top of a connection design that remains broken.

Azure Database for PostgreSQL requires encrypted connections, and disabling TLS to shave handshake time would be a serious security regression for a modest saving. The handshake is only paid once per pooled connection anyway.

A stored procedure does not reduce connection setup, which happens before any statement is sent, and the query itself is already only 4 ms. This optimises the part of the request that is not the problem.
principle: amortise connection setup with a pool instead of paying it per request
relatedConcept: Connection optimization targets the fixed per-connection costs — handshake, TLS, authentication — that dominate short, fast queries.
overallExplanation: Setup costs are paid per connection, so a per-request connect/close pattern makes a 4 ms query into a 71 ms request. Use a pool created at startup with a warm minimum; disabling TLS or moving logic server-side does not touch the handshake and authentication cost.

question: A product-recommendation API uses cache-aside against Azure Managed Redis, storing each response under `rec:{userSegment}` with a 10-minute TTL. Every ten minutes the popular segments expire simultaneously and several thousand concurrent requests all miss, all call the embedding and ranking pipeline, and downstream latency spikes to 6 seconds. What is the most effective mitigation?
options: Add jitter to each key's TTL and guard recomputation with a short-lived per-key lock so only one caller regenerates a value
Remove the TTL so cached recommendations never expire and the recomputation spike cannot occur
Increase the cache size so more segments fit in memory and fewer requests result in a miss
Retry the failing requests with exponential backoff until a populated cache entry becomes available
optionExplanations: Correct. Identical TTLs written at the same time expire together, producing a synchronised stampede; randomising the TTL spreads expiries out, and a per-key lock (or single-flight guard) ensures that when a key does expire, one caller recomputes while the rest wait briefly or serve the previous value. Together they address both the synchronisation and the fan-out.

Removing expiry stops the stampede but guarantees permanently stale recommendations and unbounded memory growth until eviction starts discarding keys unpredictably. Correctness and capacity are both sacrificed to avoid a solvable concurrency problem.

Cache size is not the constraint: the entries were present and then expired on schedule, so they were not evicted for lack of memory. More memory would not change the moment of expiry or the resulting fan-out.

Backoff retries reduce pressure only after the pipeline is already overwhelmed, and they lengthen the very latency the users are experiencing. It is a symptom-level control that leaves the synchronised expiry in place.
principle: uniform TTLs synchronise misses — jitter them and single-flight the refill
relatedConcept: Cache-aside behaviour under load is governed by expiry patterns as much as by hit rate, and stampedes are the classic failure mode.
overallExplanation: Identical TTLs make popular keys expire together and stampede the origin. Add jitter so expiries spread out and use a per-key lock so a single caller recomputes each value; removing TTLs or adding memory addresses neither the synchronisation nor the fan-out.

question: A pricing assistant caches catalogue lookups in Azure Managed Redis with a 30-minute TTL. After merchandisers change a price in the system of record, customers keep receiving the old price for up to half an hour, and the business requires the change to be visible within seconds. Which two changes achieve that? (Choose two.)
options: Delete or overwrite the affected cache keys as part of the same workflow that commits the price change
Include a version or updated-at marker in the cache key so a price change makes previously cached entries unreachable
Rely on the maxmemory eviction policy to remove outdated entries once memory pressure builds
Enable data persistence on the cache so restarts do not reintroduce values that were already superseded
optionExplanations: Correct. TTL bounds worst-case staleness but says nothing about when the source actually changes; active invalidation on write is what converts a 30-minute window into a sub-second one. Publishing the invalidation from the same workflow that commits the change keeps cache and source of record coupled at the point where they can diverge.

Correct. Versioned keys make invalidation implicit: a write that bumps the version means every subsequent read looks up a key that does not exist yet, so it misses and repopulates. Stale entries simply age out under their own TTL and can never be served again.

Eviction is a memory-pressure mechanism with no relationship to data correctness — it removes whichever keys the policy selects, which may well be fresh ones while stale entries survive. Depending on it for freshness gives you no bound at all.

Persistence controls whether data survives a restart; it neither detects source changes nor removes outdated values. If anything, persisting stale prices makes them survive a restart that would previously have cleared them.
principle: TTL bounds staleness, but only invalidation on write removes it
relatedConcept: Cache-aside correctness depends on pairing expiry with an explicit invalidation path triggered by writes to the system of record.
overallExplanation: Bound staleness with TTL, but eliminate it by invalidating on write: delete or overwrite affected keys in the same workflow that commits the change, or embed a version in the key so old entries become unreachable. Eviction policy and persistence address neither.

question: An agent platform stores each user's running tool-approval ledger only in Azure Managed Redis, under keys with no expiry, with the eviction policy set to allkeys-lru. After a memory-pressure event, several users' ledgers vanish and an audit cannot reconstruct which approvals were granted. What is the correct architectural correction?
options: Write the ledger to a durable store such as Azure Cosmos DB or PostgreSQL and keep Redis as a read cache in front of it
Change the eviction policy to volatile-lru so keys without a TTL are protected from eviction under memory pressure
Enable append-only persistence on the cache so evicted keys can be restored from the persisted file after the event
Scale the cache to a larger tier so memory pressure never triggers eviction for this workload again
optionExplanations: Correct. Redis is a cache, not a system of record: under memory pressure, failover or scaling operations, data can be evicted or lost, and no configuration turns it into an auditable ledger. Auditable state belongs in a durable transactional store, with Redis in front of it for latency.

volatile-lru would indeed skip keys with no TTL, but that converts eviction into out-of-memory write failures once the ledger fills the cache, and it still offers no durability across failover or scaling. It changes the failure mode rather than protecting the data.

Persistence improves recovery from a restart but does not undo eviction — evicted keys are removed from the dataset and are not resurrected from the persisted file. It addresses a different failure than the one described.

A bigger tier postpones the problem while the ledger grows without bound, and it does nothing for the failover and maintenance events that also disrupt cached data. Capacity is not a substitute for durability guarantees.
principle: redis is a cache, never the system of record for data you must not lose
relatedConcept: Choosing what may live only in Redis is a durability decision: cached derivations yes, authoritative state no.
overallExplanation: Auditable state must live in a durable store, with Redis as a latency layer in front. Eviction policy changes, persistence and larger tiers alter the failure mode but never make a cache an acceptable system of record.

question: A semantic cache in Azure Managed Redis embeds each incoming prompt, searches cached prompt vectors, and returns the stored answer when cosine similarity is at least 0.80. Support reports that "How do I cancel my policy?" is being answered with the cached response for "How do I cancel my payment method?". Cache hit rate is 62%. What is the appropriate adjustment?
options: Raise the similarity threshold and validate the new value against a labelled set of prompt pairs, accepting a lower hit rate
Keep the threshold and shorten the cached entries' TTL so incorrect matches are evicted sooner
Switch the distance metric from cosine to Euclidean, which separates unrelated prompts more reliably
Return the two closest cached answers and let the model choose between them at generation time
optionExplanations: Correct. The threshold is the precision/recall dial of a semantic cache: 0.80 is loose enough that topically adjacent but semantically different questions collide. Raising it and validating against labelled near-miss pairs trades hit rate for correctness, which is the right direction when wrong answers are being served.

TTL controls how long an entry lives, not which entries match. A shorter TTL means the same wrong match simply happens against a fresher entry, while overall hit rate falls — cost without correctness.

Switching metrics changes the numeric scale of the threshold rather than the underlying semantics, and for normalized text embeddings cosine and Euclidean rank neighbours nearly identically. It would require re-tuning the threshold anyway without fixing the collision.

Handing the model two cached answers reintroduces a generation call, which defeats the cache's purpose, and it invites the model to blend an irrelevant answer into the response. It adds cost and a new failure mode instead of resolving the matching error.
principle: a semantic cache threshold is a precision dial, and wrong answers cost more than misses
relatedConcept: Semantic caching keys entries by embedding similarity, so the threshold defines what counts as "the same question" and must be validated, not guessed.
overallExplanation: Serving another question's answer means the similarity threshold is too permissive. Raise it and validate against labelled near-miss pairs, accepting a lower hit rate; TTL, distance metric and multi-answer returns do not change which entries match.

question: A multi-tenant SaaS assistant uses one semantic cache in Azure Managed Redis for all customers, storing prompt embedding, answer text and a `tenantId` field per entry. A security review finds that a question asked by tenant A can return an answer generated from tenant B's private documents. Which design change resolves this?
options: Scope every similarity search to the caller's tenant with a tenant filter in the query, and include the tenant in the key prefix
Encrypt the cached answer text at rest so that entries belonging to other tenants cannot be read if returned
Reduce the cache TTL to five minutes so cross-tenant answers can only be served for a short window
Store one embedding per tenant-agnostic canonical question so answers are generic and safe to share
optionExplanations: Correct. Storing tenantId on the entry is useless unless the retrieval path enforces it, so the tenant must be part of the query — a filter combined with the vector search — and reflected in the key prefix so keyspaces are separable for both lookup and bulk invalidation. Isolation has to be enforced where matching happens, not merely recorded.

Encryption at rest protects against someone reading the underlying storage; it does nothing when the application itself decrypts and returns an entry it should never have matched. The failure is an authorization defect, not a storage-confidentiality one.
Shortening the TTL narrows the exposure window but leaves cross-tenant answers reachable within it, which no security review would accept. Time-boxing a data-leak path is not the same as closing it.

Forcing generic answers throws away the tenant-specific grounding that makes the assistant useful, and it does not prevent tenant-specific content from being cached in the first place. It solves the leak by removing the feature.
principle: isolation must be enforced in the lookup path, not stored as a field
relatedConcept: Semantic caches inherit the isolation requirements of the data that produced their entries, so tenancy belongs in both the key and the search filter.
overallExplanation: Enforce tenancy where matching happens: filter similarity searches by tenant and prefix keys per tenant so keyspaces are separable. A tenantId field that no query checks provides no isolation, and encryption or short TTLs do not close the path.

question: A documentation assistant caches generated answers semantically in Azure Managed Redis with a 24-hour TTL. The underlying knowledge base is re-indexed nightly, and after each re-index users continue to receive answers built from the previous corpus for most of the following day. The team wants correctness immediately after every re-index without abandoning the cache. What should they do?
options: Include the corpus version in the cache key prefix and index name, and cut over to the new prefix when re-indexing completes
Reduce the TTL to one hour so stale answers disappear soon after the nightly re-index finishes
Warm the cache immediately after each re-index by replaying yesterday's most frequent questions
Disable the semantic cache during the re-index window and re-enable it once the new index is live
optionExplanations: Correct. Versioning the keyspace makes cutover atomic from the reader's point of view: after re-indexing, lookups target the new prefix, immediately miss, and regenerate from the current corpus, while the old keyspace ages out under its TTL or is deleted in the background. Correctness stops depending on expiry timing.

A one-hour TTL still serves stale answers for up to an hour after every re-index and multiplies regeneration cost across the entire day for every entry. It weakens the cache badly while leaving a stale window that the requirement rules out.

Warming populates entries but does nothing about the ones already cached from the old corpus, which continue to match incoming questions until their TTL expires. It adds cost on top of the staleness rather than removing it.

Disabling the cache during re-indexing addresses only the window in which the index is being rebuilt; the entries generated before it remain valid-looking afterwards. The stale answers users see arrive after re-indexing, not during it.
principle: version the cache keyspace so a source change invalidates everything at once
relatedConcept: Semantic cache entries are derived data, so their lifetime must be tied to the version of the corpus that produced them rather than to elapsed time.
overallExplanation: Tie cached answers to the corpus version by putting the version in the key prefix and index name, so a re-index cuts over to an empty keyspace and old entries can never match. TTL tuning, warming and pausing the cache all leave stale entries reachable.

objective: Integrate Azure Managed Redis in AI solutions
question: A team enables the query engine on Azure Managed Redis to serve similarity search over 2.5 million product embeddings of 768 dimensions, with a p99 target of 25 ms and tolerance for approximate results. Their prototype index was created with a FLAT vector field and now takes about 400 ms per KNN query. What should they change?
options: Recreate the index with an HNSW vector field so KNN queries traverse a graph instead of scanning every vector
Keep the FLAT index and reduce K from 10 to 3 so fewer neighbours must be compared per query
Shard the keyspace across more nodes and issue the same KNN query to each shard from the client
Store the embeddings as JSON documents rather than hashes, which lets the engine compress the vector field
optionExplanations: Correct. A FLAT vector field performs exact brute-force comparison against every indexed vector, so its latency grows linearly with the collection and 2.5 million vectors is far past its comfortable range. HNSW builds a navigable graph that returns approximate neighbours in roughly logarithmic time, which is exactly the trade the team has already said they accept.

K barely affects the cost of a FLAT search: the distance is still computed against all 2.5 million vectors, and only the size of the result heap changes. The scan dominates, so latency stays close to 400 ms.

Sharding spreads vectors across nodes and can reduce per-node work, but each shard still brute-force scans its slice and the client must merge results. It buys a constant factor at considerable complexity, where the algorithm choice offers an order of magnitude.

The storage model — hash or JSON — determines how documents are laid out, not which search algorithm the vector field uses. A FLAT field on JSON documents scans exhaustively exactly as it does on hashes.
principle: flat vector indexes are exact and linear; hnsw is approximate and scalable
relatedConcept: Redis vector indexing exposes the same exact-versus-approximate choice as other vector stores, decided when the index is created.
overallExplanation: FLAT vector fields scan every vector, so latency scales with collection size. With 2.5 million vectors, a 25 ms target and tolerance for approximation, recreate the index with an HNSW vector field; reducing K, sharding or changing the document type do not change the scan.

objective: Integrate Azure Managed Redis in AI solutions
question: A customer-service agent keeps per-conversation state — recent turns, the active tool context and a summary — in Azure Managed Redis so any stateless API replica can continue a conversation. The team must keep memory bounded while ensuring a completed conversation can still be reviewed months later for quality assurance. Which two practices should they adopt? (Choose two.)
options: Keep each conversation in its own key or hash with an expiry that is refreshed on every turn, so idle conversations age out
Persist the completed transcript to a durable store at the end of the conversation, treating Redis as working state only
Remove expiry from conversation keys and rely on the cache's eviction policy to reclaim memory when needed
Store the entire transcript in one string value and rewrite the whole value on every turn to keep reads simple
optionExplanations: Correct. A per-conversation key with an expiry refreshed on each turn implements a sliding session window: active conversations stay resident and abandoned ones release memory automatically, without a sweeper job. It also keeps reads and writes scoped to a single key, which is what stateless replicas need for fast resumption.

Correct. Redis is working state that can be expired, evicted or lost across scaling and failover, so anything needed months later must be written to a durable store. Persisting the transcript on completion separates the latency-sensitive live path from the long-term record.

Without expiry, abandoned conversations accumulate indefinitely, and eviction then discards keys chosen by policy — quite possibly active conversations — producing user-visible state loss at the worst moment. Eviction is a memory-pressure valve, not a retention design.

Rewriting a growing transcript on every turn makes each write cost proportional to conversation length and produces large values that block other work as they are serialized. A hash or list of turns lets the agent append and read the recent window cheaply.
principle: session state expires; the record of it must be persisted elsewhere
relatedConcept: Conversation state in Redis is a sliding-window working set, which makes expiry policy and durable hand-off two halves of the same design.
overallExplanation: Give each conversation its own key with an expiry refreshed per turn so idle sessions age out, and persist the completed transcript to a durable store because Redis can expire, evict or lose it. Relying on eviction or rewriting one giant value creates both memory and correctness problems.

domain: Develop AI solutions by using Azure data management services
objective: Integrate Azure Managed Redis in AI solutions
question: An index in Azure Managed Redis was created over hash keys with the prefix `doc:` and a vector field for embeddings. After a refactor, an ingestion worker began writing new chunks under keys prefixed `chunk:`, with an identical field layout. Similarity searches return only pre-refactor documents, and no errors appear in the worker's logs. What is the cause?
options: The index only tracks keys matching the prefixes declared when it was created, so documents under a new prefix are never indexed
The index must be manually refreshed after bulk writes, and the worker never triggers the reindex operation
The new keys were written without a TTL, and the index only tracks keys that carry an expiry
The vector field on the new keys is stored in a different byte order, so the index silently rejects those documents
optionExplanations: Correct. The index definition specifies the key type and the prefixes it follows, and indexing is automatic only for keys that match. Writes under `chunk:` fall entirely outside the index's scope, so they succeed silently and never become searchable — which is precisely the observed pattern of no errors and no new results.

Indexing happens automatically as matching keys are written; there is no manual refresh step to forget. If a refresh were required, previously written documents would also be missing rather than only the post-refactor ones.

TTL has no bearing on whether a key is indexed; expiry removes documents from the index only when it actually fires. Pre-refactor documents would have to carry TTLs for this theory to hold, and nothing suggests they do.

The worker writes vectors the same way it always did — only the key prefix changed — and a genuine encoding mismatch would surface as indexing errors or wrong distances rather than silent absence. This invents a failure mode to explain a scoping problem.
principle: an index covers exactly the key prefixes it was defined over
relatedConcept: Redis vector indexes are defined at creation time against a key type and prefix set, so key-naming changes silently change what is searchable.
overallExplanation: A Redis index automatically tracks only keys matching the prefixes in its definition, so documents written under a new prefix are stored but never searchable. Either keep the agreed prefix or recreate the index to cover it.
